title: Intermountain Electronics Inc. v. Commissioner
subject: Pilot Models and Documentation Standards
summary: Intermountain Electronics v. Commissioner is a U.S. Tax Court case in which Judge Ronald L. Buch, in a March 14, 2024 order, denied the IRS's partial summary judgment motion, holding that pilot model production costs are not categorically excluded from the 80% "substantially all" numerator under IRC Section 41, though taxpayers must prove a process of experimentation at trial.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background

In Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 11019-19 (T.C. Order Mar. 14, 2024), the United States Tax Court issued a pivotal order denying the Internal Revenue Service’s (IRS) motion for partial summary judgment regarding the eligibility of pilot model production expenses for the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. Presided over by Judge Ronald L. Buch, the ruling addresses one of the most contentious battlegrounds in federal tax controversy: whether physical manufacturing, fabrication, and assembly costs incurred in producing custom "pilot models" under IRC Section 174 are categorically excluded from the numerator of the 80% "substantially all" process-of-experimentation fraction under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C).
Taxpayer Operations and the R&D Credit Claim

Intermountain Electronics, Inc. (Intermountain) is a Utah-based C corporation engaged in the custom design, engineering, fabrication, assembly, and servicing of specialized electrical distribution and control equipment. Serving heavy industrial sectors including surface and underground mining, oil and gas refining, power generation, and government contracting, Intermountain’s core operational lines encompass custom equipment fabrication, transformer production, and proprietary product innovation, such as custom switchgear, specialized control systems, and modular electrical houses ("e-houses"). Intermountain’s end-to-end product lifecycle spans initial conceptual and electrical engineering design, in-house component fabrication, physical assembly, and final factory testing prior to customer acceptance and deployment.

For the 2012 through 2015 tax years, Intermountain claimed federal R&D tax credits under IRC Section 41 based on qualified research expenses (QREs) incurred in designing and manufacturing its custom electrical equipment. The claimed QREs included wages paid to non-production personnel (such as electrical and mechanical engineers), wages paid to production personnel (such as shop-floor fabricators, machinists, and assemblers), and raw material supply costs consumed during fabrication. Intermountain premised its claim on the legal theory that each custom electrical distribution and control system constituted a unique, nonrepeatable finished design that qualified in its entirety as a "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Consequently, Intermountain contended that its physical production processes were an integral part of an evaluative process undertaken to resolve technological uncertainty relating to the development of custom electrical equipment.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following examination, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue disallowed Intermountain’s claimed R&D tax credits and moved for partial summary judgment pursuant to U.S. Tax Court Rule 121(a)(2). The IRS sought a ruling as a matter of law that Intermountain was ineligible for the Section 41 credit based on two interrelated statutory challenges. First, the IRS contended that Intermountain’s physical production costs for the custom units were ordinary manufacturing expenses rather than eligible research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under IRC Section 174 and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), which mandate that qualifying costs be incurred in an "experimental or laboratory sense". Second, the IRS argued that Intermountain’s pilot models failed the "substantially all" test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).

Relying heavily on the Tax Court’s earlier memorandum opinion in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (subsequently affirmed on evidentiary grounds by the Seventh Circuit at 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)), the IRS asserted that production expenses—such as physical component fabrication and assembly labor—are categorically excluded from the numerator of the 80% "substantially all" equation, even if they are included in the denominator of total project research costs. Because Intermountain’s non-production engineering costs accounted for less than 80% of the total costs incurred on the claimed pilot models, the Commissioner argued that excluding production expenses from the numerator made it mathematically impossible for Intermountain to satisfy the 80% threshold required by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6).
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

To evaluate the Commissioner’s motion, the Tax Court analyzed the intersecting requirements of IRC Sections 41 and 174 and their corresponding Treasury Regulations. Under IRC Section 41(d)(1), an activity constitutes "qualified research" only if it is not an excluded activity under Section 41(d)(4) and satisfies a cumulative four-part statutory test applied separately to each defined "business component".

Under the first prong, the Section 174 Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)), the expenditures connected with the activity must be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174. Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent R&D costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a "pilot model" as "any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product," explicitly including "a fully functional representation or model of the product". While the 2012–2015 tax years at issue in Intermountain are governed by pre-TCJA Section 174 rules, the underlying definition of R&E expenditures remains foundational across both the post-2021 Section 174 mandatory amortization regime and the Section 174A domestic deduction provisions enacted in 2025 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024.

Under the second and third prongs—the Technological in Nature Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i)) and the Business Component / Permitted Purpose Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A))—the research must be undertaken to discover information that fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science, and the taxpayer must intend that the discovered information be useful in developing a new or improved business component (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer’s trade or business) for improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Under the fourth prong, the Process of Experimentation and "Substantially All" Test (IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)), substantially all of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) defines a process of experimentation as an evaluative process patterned on the scientific method that identifies uncertainty, identifies one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and conducts a process of evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) defines "substantially all" quantitatively, requiring that 80% or more of a taxpayer’s research activities for a given business component—measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose:

Furthermore, in determining which employee wages and supply costs enter this calculation, IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c) divide "qualified services" into three distinct activity levels: engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research (direct engagement); engaging in the immediate, "one-up" supervision of qualified research (direct supervision); and engaging in the direct support of research, such as a machinist machining a part of an experimental model or a laboratory worker cleaning research equipment.
The Court's Holding and Jurisprudential Significance

In its March 14, 2024 Order, the Tax Court denied the Commissioner’s motion for partial summary judgment, dismantling the IRS’s attempt to weaponize Little Sandy Coal as a per se legal bar against production QREs. Judge Buch held that Little Sandy Coal Co. "does not foreclose production expenses from being included in the numerator of the substantially all equation," adding specifically that "[n]othing in that statement forecloses a finding that a production worker is directly engaged in qualified research".

The Tax Court clarified that in Little Sandy Coal, the taxpayer’s ship-construction labor was excluded from the numerator not because production costs are categorically disqualified by statute or regulation, but because that specific taxpayer failed as an evidentiary matter to establish a factual nexus between fabricating the physical vessel and conducting an evaluative test. Although Judge Buch’s order did not explicitly cite the Seventh Circuit’s appellate ruling in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the Tax Court’s order is consistent with the Seventh Circuit’s conclusion that pilot model production costs can be included in the numerator of the 80% fraction when they constitute elements of a process of experimentation; however, the order did not adopt the Seventh Circuit’s broader holding that direct support and direct supervision activities may populate both the numerator and the denominator, and its emphasis that a production worker may be “directly engaged” in qualified research leaves open whether the Tax Court continues to limit the numerator to direct research activities.

Because pilot model production costs are not categorically excluded from the numerator as a matter of law, the Tax Court concluded that "[g]enuine disputes of material fact remain as to whether Intermountain’s production activities constituted a process of experimentation". While the March 14, 2024 ruling preserved Intermountain’s claim for trial, the Court underscored that eligibility remains an intensive question of fact requiring granular proof at trial. Subsequent orders in the docket—including a May 30, 2024 order resolving a Tax Court Rule 91(f) stipulation and exhibit dispute, and an August 24, 2026 post-trial order holding that Intermountain waived a Loper Bright challenge to the Treasury Regulations by failing to raise it until its reply brief—demonstrate the procedural rigor applied by the Tax Court once a case moves past summary judgment to trial on the merits; notably, in the May 30, 2024 order the Court rejected the Commissioner’s proposed edits to the stipulations and allowed Intermountain to make the referenced exhibits available to the Court rather than attaching them.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

While Intermountain defeated the Commissioner’s categorical legal argument at the summary judgment stage, the dispute—and the broader wave of IRS enforcement targeting custom manufacturers—was triggered by severe structural, technical, contractual, and evidentiary vulnerabilities in how the R&D tax credit claim was constructed and litigated. An examination of the March 14, 2024 Order alongside the subsequent docket orders and controlling federal precedent reveals five core legal and evidentiary failures that expose custom manufacturers to disallowance.
Improper "All-or-Nothing" Business Component Aggregation and Pilot Model Overreach

The foundational flaw that precipitated the IRS challenge was Intermountain’s decision to define each entire custom electrical equipment unit—such as complete modular e-houses, transformers, and switchgear assemblies—as a single, unified "pilot model" business component under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Intermountain asserted that because each custom unit represented a unique, nonrepeatable finished design tailored to specific operational parameters, the entire physical unit constituted a pilot model, thereby pulling all non-production design hours, all shop-floor fabrication and assembly wages, and all raw material supply costs into the QRE calculation.

This "all-or-nothing" macro-component strategy directly triggers the mathematical trap of the 80% "substantially all" rule under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), a product unit is not a pilot model merely because it is custom-engineered, bespoke, or first-of-its-kind; as the Seventh Circuit emphasized in Little Sandy Coal, "the novelty of a business component is not a proper heuristic for the substantially all test". A full-scale unit qualifies as a pilot model only if it is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during the development or improvement of the product; as the Seventh Circuit explained, a prototype alone is not enough—the model must actually be used to evaluate one or more alternatives through a process of experimentation.

When a custom manufacturer defines the business component as the entire multi-ton electrical enclosure or transformer assembly, the denominator of the 80% fraction becomes saturated with thousands of hours of routine structural steel fabrication, standard sheet-metal bending, commercial painting, conduit routing, and off-the-shelf component mounting. If technological uncertainty actually resides only within a specific sub-assembly—such as a novel harmonic filtering circuit, an arc-resistant venting mechanism, or a high-altitude thermal dissipation core—claiming the entire unit prevents the taxpayer from satisfying the 80% threshold unless it properly invokes the "shrinking-back" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). By failing to segregate and document costs at the sub-component level from the outset, a taxpayer that "swings for the fences" on whole-unit pilot models risks total disallowance when the macro component fails the 80% fraction.
Conflation of Initial Design Uncertainty with Shop-Floor Process of Experimentation

A critical legal risk—one that the Tax Court’s March 14, 2024 Order did not resolve but left for trial as a genuine dispute of material fact—is the failure to distinguish between resolving uncertainty during the engineering design phase and conducting a process of experimentation during the physical production phase. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) explicitly warns taxpayers that "[u]ncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component (e.g., its appropriate design) does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation".

In custom electrical manufacturing, engineering teams routinely encounter technological uncertainty regarding appropriate design when translating customer load specifications into electrical schematics and 3D CAD models. However, in standard industrial workflows, engineers resolve those uncertainties using engineering calculations, finite element analysis (FEA), thermal modeling, and load-flow simulations prior to releasing final shop drawings to the manufacturing floor. Once the appropriate design is established and released for fabrication, the technological uncertainty has been eliminated.

If shop-floor production workers are merely cutting steel, winding coils, and wiring switchgear in accordance with finalized engineering blueprints, their production labor is commercial manufacturing excluded under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(A), not an element of a process of experimentation. Similarly, when the completed unit undergoes final inspection and testing prior to customer approval, routine Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) or quality control verification to confirm that the unit was built to specification does not retroactively transform the preceding fabrication labor into an experiment. As the Tax Court made clear in denying summary judgment, production costs are not categorically excluded from the numerator of the 80% fraction, but whether Intermountain’s production activities constituted a process of experimentation is a genuine dispute of material fact that the taxpayer must prove at trial; consistent with the Seventh Circuit’s reasoning in Little Sandy Coal, the physical fabrication must be shown to be part of an evaluative process used to test and evaluate design alternatives, not merely the construction of a prototype.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation Linking Production Labor and Supplies to Experimental Activities

The Tax Court’s March 14, 2024 Order established that whether production expenses belong in the numerator of the "substantially all" fraction is a question of fact requiring rigorous substantiation at trial. In both Little Sandy Coal and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, taxpayers suffered total disallowance for evidentiary failures: in Little Sandy Coal, the Seventh Circuit affirmed because the taxpayer did not offer a "principled way to determine what portion of the employee activities for each vessel" constituted elements of a process of experimentation, while in Betz the taxpayers failed to establish that their products were pilot models, kept no contemporaneous time records for employees, and could not rely on after-the-fact Cohan estimates of employee time.

In Intermountain’s operational environment, claiming wages for both non-production and production staff across custom projects created an acute substantiation deficit across three dimensions. First, regarding the blurring of activity levels under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), to include production personnel in the numerator, the taxpayer must prove through project records that specific shop-floor workers were either directly engaged in executing experimental tests or providing direct support (under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)) by machining or assembling a specific experimental prototype component. Broad, retrospective percentage allocations or general oral testimony asserting that shop-floor fabricators "collaborated with engineers" are routinely rejected by the Tax Court. Second, regarding supply QREs under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(C), when claiming raw materials and electrical components on custom equipment sold to customers, taxpayers frequently fail to segregate materials consumed in destructive testing, iterative prototyping, or uncertain sub-assemblies from standard commercial bill-of-materials (BOM) inventory incorporated into the final commercial unit. Third, standard job-costing ERP systems track hours by job or work order rather than by scientific hypothesis or design iteration. Without contemporaneous Engineering Change Notices (ECNs), prototype test logs, failure analysis reports, and timecards segregated between experimental rework and standard build tasks, the taxpayer cannot mathematically substantiate that the numerator of its activities reached or exceeded the 80% threshold.
Vulnerability to Statutory Exclusions: Adaptation, Duplication, and Funded Research

Custom equipment manufacturers operating across mining, oil and gas, power generation, and government sectors face severe exposure under the statutory exclusions of IRC Section 41(d)(4). Many custom electrical enclosures, transformers, and switchgear assemblies are engineered by scaling or configuring pre-existing proprietary templates or modular platforms to meet a specific customer’s voltage, footprint, or environmental specifications. Under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3), adapting an existing business component to a particular customer’s requirement or need is categorically excluded from qualified research unless the adaptation itself requires resolving fundamental technological uncertainty through a process of experimentation.

Simultaneously, because Intermountain engineered and fabricated custom equipment pursuant to customer orders and government contracts, custom projects are heavily scrutinized under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) to determine whether the research is "funded" by a third party. Under established federal precedent—including Fairchild Industries, Lockheed Martin, Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and Betz—a contractor’s research is disqualified as funded unless payment is contingent on the technical success of the research (the financial risk test) and the taxpayer retains "substantial rights" in the research results (the intellectual property test). Custom fabrication contracts that utilize progress billings not tied to technical acceptance criteria, or customer terms and conditions that assign all custom schematics and design rights exclusively to the customer without reserving a royalty-free license for the manufacturer, automatically disqualify the underlying QREs.
Procedural, Stipulation, and Briefing Failures During Litigation

Beyond substantive tax law deficiencies, the docket history of Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner (Docket No. 11019-19) exposes two litigation episodes after the March 14, 2024 summary judgment order—a contested stipulation dispute and a waived regulatory challenge—that illustrate the procedural demands of Tax Court litigation. First, under U.S. Tax Court Rule 91(a), parties are required to stipulate, to the fullest extent to which complete or qualified agreement can or fairly should be reached, all relevant matters that are not privileged. Following the denial of partial summary judgment, Intermountain and the IRS became locked in a contentious Rule 91(f) motion to compel stipulation resolved by Judge Buch on May 30, 2024, involving 35 separate stipulations of fact and voluminous underlying exhibits. In that dispute, the Commissioner objected to 14 of the 35 proposed stipulations because they referred to exhibits that were not attached, although he did not dispute the truth of the stipulated facts or that he had seen the referenced documents; Judge Buch rejected the Commissioner’s proposed text edits because they did not state the sources, reasons, or basis required by Rule 91(f)(2), and permitted Intermountain to make the exhibits available to the Court rather than attaching them. The episode nonetheless shows that failing to agree in advance on a clean, indexed set of stipulated exhibits forces judicial intervention and consumes pre-trial resources.

Second, the trial in Intermountain Electronics generated thousands of pages of transcript and exhibits. Two days after the trial concluded—and more than three months before Intermountain filed its Seriatim Opening Brief—the U.S. Supreme Court issued its landmark decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024), overruling Chevron deference and empowering taxpayers to challenge the validity of Treasury Regulations (such as the strict 80% mathematical fraction in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) or the pilot model rules in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)) as exceeding statutory authority. Despite having more than three months to incorporate Loper Bright arguments into its Seriatim Opening Brief, Intermountain failed to do so, attempting instead to raise a Loper Bright regulatory challenge for the first time in its post-trial reply brief. In an Order issued August 24, 2026, Judge Buch admonished Intermountain and refused to consider the argument, citing Ashkouri v. Commissioner and Considine v. Commissioner, 74 T.C. 955, 969–70 (1980), for the strict procedural rule that legal issues raised for the first time in a reply brief are untimely and waived.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement implicated in Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner against the specific taxpayer vulnerabilities and the controlling standard of proof enforced by the U.S. Tax Court.

headers: U.S. Tax Court Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Burden

cells: Section 174 Eligibility & Pilot Model Definition IRC § 41(d)(1)(A); IRC § 174; Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), (a)(4)

Treating every custom-designed, unique, and nonrepeatable commercial unit (e.g., e-houses, transformers, switchgear) in its entirety as a "pilot model" despite the unit being fabricated primarily for commercial delivery rather than experimental evaluation.

The taxpayer must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the physical model was produced specifically to evaluate and resolve technological uncertainty (capability, method, or appropriate design) concerning the product during its development or improvement, and that the model was actually used to evaluate design alternatives rather than merely delivered as the commercial product.
Business Component Definition & Shrinking-Back Rule IRC § 41(d)(2)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)

Adopting an "all-or-nothing" macro business component definition (claiming the entire custom equipment unit) without isolating specific uncertain sub-assemblies or sub-components, thereby flooding the cost pool with routine structural and assembly labor.

If the macro product fails the four-part test (specifically the 80% process-of-experimentation threshold), the taxpayer must provide granular cost and activity records isolating the most significant subset of elements (sub-component) that independently satisfies all four statutory tests.
Process of Experimentation (Evaluative Methodology) IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); IRC § 41(d)(3)(A); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i)

Relying solely on the existence of initial design uncertainty or product novelty to claim that subsequent shop-floor fabrication and routine Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT) automatically constitute a process of experimentation.

Mere design uncertainty does not establish a process of experimentation. The taxpayer must substantiate a structured, scientific methodology that identifies specific technical uncertainties, formulates competing design alternatives or hypotheses, and systematically evaluates those alternatives through modeling, simulation, or iterative physical testing.
The "Substantially All" (80%) Fraction Numerator IRC § 41(d)(1)(C); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)

Including large volumes of shop-floor production labor in the project cost pool without proving that those production activities were part of an evaluative experiment, risking mathematical failure if production costs are excluded from the numerator while remaining in the denominator.

Production costs are not categorically excluded from the numerator as a matter of law (Intermountain rejection of the IRS’s reading of Little Sandy Coal). However, inclusion is a strict question of fact: the taxpayer must prove at trial that at least 80% of total research costs for the business component (including claimed production labor) constituted elements of a process of experimentation.
Qualified Services: Direct Engagement, Supervision & Support IRC § 41(b)(2)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3)

Claiming broad wage allocations for production workers, machinists, and shop supervisors without differentiating between commercial fabrication according to finalized blueprints and direct support of experimental prototypes.

The taxpayer must establish a factual nexus for each employee activity level, demonstrating that production workers were either directly engaged in testing or performing direct support (e.g., machining a specific part for an experimental model under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)) rather than routine production.
Exclusion for Adaptation of Existing Components IRC § 41(d)(4)(B); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3)

Claiming R&D credits for routine custom engineering that configures, scales, or modifies pre-existing electrical designs to fit a specific customer’s site, voltage, or dimensional requirements using established engineering formulas.

The taxpayer must prove that existing knowledge and standard engineering calculations could not establish the capability, method, or appropriate design, requiring fundamental technological experimentation beyond mere customer adaptation.
Exclusion for Funded Research IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)

Performing custom design and fabrication under customer purchase orders or government contracts where milestone payments are guaranteed regardless of technical success or where the contract assigns all design IP exclusively to the customer.

The taxpayer must prove through executed contract provisions that (1) payment is contingent upon the technical success of the research (the taxpayer bears financial risk of rework/rejection), and (2) the taxpayer retains substantial rights to use the resulting technology in its business without paying royalties.
Contemporaneous Substantiation & Recordkeeping IRC § 6001; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d); Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1
Relying on high-level ERP job-cost buckets, uncorroborated post-hoc employee interviews, and disorganized multi-thousand-page document dumps that trigger Rule 91(f) stipulation disputes.

While no single timekeeping system is mandated, the taxpayer must present organized, usable project records, engineering documentation, and a principled cost-allocation methodology that reliably links specific wages and supplies to qualified experimental activities at the component or sub-component level.
Timely Preservation of Regulatory Challenges (Loper Bright) Tax Court Rule 151; Considine v. Commissioner, 74 T.C. 955 (1980)

Failing to challenge the statutory validity of Treasury Regulations under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo in the post-trial Seriatim Opening Brief and attempting to raise the challenge for the first time in a reply brief.
Under settled Tax Court precedent, legal and administrative law arguments not timely raised and preserved in the opening brief are deemed waived and will not be considered by the Court.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings and evidentiary standards of Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. Commissioner into actionable tax governance, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic engineering and custom fabrication projects that exhibit the exact vulnerabilities challenged by the IRS. Each case study provides a comprehensive, step-by-step remedial blueprint covering project governance, technical documentation, contract restructuring, and shop-floor cost tracking.
Case Study 1: Custom Medium-Voltage Mining Substation ("E-House") and Arc-Resistant Switchgear
Project Scenario and Initial Vulnerability Profile

Apex Power Systems, Inc. (Apex), a domestic C corporation, is contracted by a western U.S. underground copper mining operator to design, fabricate, and test a custom 13.8kV mobile modular electrical house ("E-House") integrated with medium-voltage arc-resistant switchgear and variable frequency drives (VFDs). The unit must operate continuously at an elevation of 11,500 feet in a high-particulate, corrosive underground environment where thin air severely degrades dielectric insulation and convective thermal cooling.

The total project cost is $1,800,000, comprising $220,000 in non-production engineering and design labor (electrical schematic design, thermal modeling, and plenum geometry calculations), $680,000 in shop-floor production fabrication and assembly labor ($560,000 for structural steel welding, exterior wall fabrication, standard HVAC installation, and routine wiring, plus $120,000 for fabricating, assembling, and iteratively modifying an experimental high-altitude pressurized arc-plenum and custom liquid-cooled busbar assembly), and $900,000 in raw materials and supplies ($750,000 for structural steel, standard transformers, and commercial breakers, plus $150,000 for specialized dielectric coatings, custom copper busbars, and sacrificial sensors consumed during high-current arc-fault and thermal-rise testing).

On its initial tax study workpapers, Apex treats the entire $1,800,000 E-House as a single "pilot model" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), claiming that the unit is a unique, nonrepeatable finished design. However, 82% of the shop-floor production labor ($560,000) and 83% of the materials ($750,000) relate to standard structural steel enclosure fabrication and off-the-shelf component integration where no technological uncertainty existed. If the IRS audits the claim, the entire $1,800,000 business component fails the 80% "substantially all" test under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) because routine structural fabrication ($560,000 labor) cannot be substantiated as an element of a process of experimentation, dropping the numerator well below 80% of total business component research activities. Furthermore, the customer’s standard purchase order includes a boilerplate clause stating that "all custom drawings, specifications, and technical data developed hereunder shall be the sole and exclusive property of Buyer," exposing the entire claim to disqualification as funded research under IRC Section 41(d)(4)(H).
Step 1: Project Governance and Pre-Emptive Shrinking-Back Segregation

Rather than claiming the entire E-House as a monolithic pilot model, Apex’s tax and engineering governance committee must apply the business component and shrinking-back rules under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) at project inception to isolate the true locus of technological uncertainty. Apex must formally exclude the structural steel skid, exterior enclosure walls, standard lighting, and commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) breakers from the R&D project scope, classifying them as standard commercial manufacturing. Simultaneously, Apex must establish two discrete sub-component business components: Sub-Component 101-A (the High-Altitude Dielectric Busbar and Liquid-Cooled Thermal Dissipation Assembly) and Sub-Component 101-B (the Compact Internal Arc-Fault Containment and Pressurized Exhaust Plenum). In the project charter, engineering leadership must document that physical fabrication of Sub-Components 101-A and 101-B qualifies under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) because multi-physics Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) software cannot accurately predict plasma arc-gas dynamics or dielectric corona discharge in 11,500-foot thin-air density, necessitating the physical construction and high-load testing of full-scale functional sub-assembly models to resolve design uncertainty.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Prove an Evaluative Process of Experimentation

To satisfy Judge Buch’s requirement that production activities be factually proven as elements of a process of experimentation, Apex must replace generic engineering release notes with a structured Experimental Test and Fabrication Protocol (ETFP) for Sub-Components 101-A and 101-B. Prior to cutting metal on the sub-components, engineers must record specific competing design hypotheses in the ETFP pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i): specifically, evaluating Alternative 1 (an epoxied aluminum busbar geometry paired with staggered baffle plates in the exhaust plenum) against Alternative 2 (a silver-plated copper busbar with fluoropolymer dielectric sleeving and a dual-stage Venturi pressure-relief damper).

To bridge engineering uncertainty to shop-floor production, Apex must issue dedicated Experimental Work Orders (EWOs) to the fabrication floor stating explicitly that the sub-assembly is an experimental prototype under active engineering evaluation rather than a released-for-construction commercial build. Instead of logging only a single pass/fail Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) prior to customer shipment, Apex must maintain contemporaneous Test Iteration Logs. In Iteration Log #1, engineers record that during simulated 11,500-foot altitude chamber testing at a 4,000A continuous load, Alternative 1 experienced corona partial discharge at 9.2kV and exceeded the 65°C thermal rise limit. Engineering Change Notice ECN-204 then directs production machinists to disassemble the busbar, machine modified Venturi damper linkages, and install Alternative 2 for Test Iteration #2, thereby establishing a seamless documentary chain between shop-floor fabrication and scientific evaluation.
Step 3: Shop-Floor Labor Segregation and Mathematical Verification of the 80% Fraction

To ensure the numerator of the "substantially all" fraction exceeds 80% under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and survives audit scrutiny under Intermountain and Little Sandy Coal, Apex must restructure its ERP job-costing and time-tracking architecture to isolate specific activity levels under IRC Section 41(b)(2)(B), as detailed in the table below.

Step 4: Contractual Restructuring to Defeat Funded Research and Adaptation Exclusions

Prior to executing the customer contract, Apex’s legal counsel must execute a Technical and Commercial Terms Addendum containing two mandatory provisions to overcome IRC Section 41(d)(4)(B) and (H). First, the addendum must incorporate a Financial Risk and Contingent Payment Clause specifying that all milestone and progress payments are temporary advances subject to full refund if Sub-Components 101-A and 101-B fail to pass rigorous high-altitude dielectric and IEEE C37.20.7 arc-containment performance criteria during acceptance testing, and explicitly stating that Apex bears 100% of the financial cost of iterative engineering, prototype rework, and material scrap required to achieve technical compliance. Second, the addendum must replace the customer’s unilateral IP assignment clause with a Reservation of Substantial Rights Clause providing that while the customer receives title to the physical E-House unit and site-specific installation drawings, Apex retains full ownership (or an irrevocable, perpetual, transferable, royalty-free license) to all underlying engineering innovations, busbar geometries, thermal management designs, and testing know-how developed during the project for use in future commercial projects.
Case Study 2: Custom Industrial High-Temperature Catalytic Thermal Oxidizer and Automated PLC Control System
Project Scenario and Initial Vulnerability Profile

Vanguard Environmental Fabrication Corp. (Vanguard) designs and manufactures custom industrial air-pollution control equipment and specialized Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) automation skids for petrochemical refineries. A refinery client contracts Vanguard under a $2,500,000 fixed-price contract to design and build a regenerative catalytic thermal oxidizer (RCTO) capable of destroying volatile organic compounds (VOCs) containing high concentrations of halogenated siloxanes without poisoning the catalyst bed or causing thermal runaway.

To develop the system, Vanguard incurs $300,000 in chemical/process engineering and PLC software development wages, $950,000 in shop-floor boilermaker, pipefitter, and assembly wages, and $1,250,000 in raw steel, refractory brick, valves, and catalyst media. Vanguard claims the entire $2,500,000 expenditure as a single pilot model business component, relying on post-year-end executive interviews estimating that "75% of all shop-floor boilermakers and pipefitters supported R&D because every vessel is custom-built".

Vanguard’s claim suffers from multiple fatal defects of the kind at issue in Intermountain Electronics and Betz v. Commissioner. First, relying on retrospective oral estimates (75% of shop labor) without contemporaneous records linking pipefitters and boilermakers to specific experimental tests fails the evidentiary burden required at trial. Second, rolling the outer carbon-steel vessel shell and laying refractory brick are standard ASME vessel fabrication activities resolved by established engineering codes (adaptation and commercial production), not experimental activities. Excluding the $950,000 of shop-floor fabrication labor from the numerator reduces Vanguard’s process-of-experimentation ratio to 16.4%, failing the 80% "substantially all" requirement. Third, Vanguard’s documentation consists of 15,000 pages of unindexed shop drawings, material purchase orders, and emails, inviting the kind of pre-trial Rule 91(f) stipulation dispute over unattached exhibits that arose in Intermountain.
Step 1: Governance Restructuring and Sub-Component Isolation

Vanguard must establish an R&D Tax Governance Gate at the Preliminary Design Review (PDR) stage to separate routine ASME vessel manufacturing from genuine technological research. The governance committee must formally carve out the carbon-steel outer housing, structural support legs, refractory lining installation, and standard exhaust stack from the Section 41 claim, recognizing that these elements are designed using established ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code formulas. Vanguard must then isolate two qualifying sub-components under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(B): Business Component 201-A (a Hardware Pilot Model comprising the Dual-Stage Siloxane Scrubber and Modular Catalyst Guard-Bed Cartridge) and Business Component 201-B (a Software/Control Component comprising the Predictive Exothermic Quench PLC Algorithm designed to prevent catalyst sintering during rapid VOC concentration spikes).
Step 2: Implementing Contemporaneous Experimentation and Production Tracking

To establish the factual nexus required by the Tax Court’s March 14, 2024 Order in Intermountain so that production labor on Component 201-A qualifies for the numerator, Vanguard must implement a Shop-Floor Experimental Traveler System. Instead of building the entire 40-foot RCTO vessel and merely turning it on at the customer’s site, Vanguard constructs a modular, full-scale functional prototype of the Guard-Bed Cartridge and Venturi Mixing Manifold (Component 201-A) for iterative testing on an in-house high-temperature gas flow loop.

Vanguard tracks each experimental iteration through dedicated shop-floor travelers. In Iteration 1, pipefitters and machinists fabricate Manifold Geometry A (a conical diffuser with ceramic honeycomb) under Traveler #EXP-201A-1; flow-loop testing with doped siloxane gas reveals uneven velocity profiles causing 35% catalyst fouling within 48 hours. In Iteration 2, engineers redesign the internal louver angles, and machinists laser-cut and weld modified helical turning vanes under Traveler #EXP-201A-2; subsequent flow-loop testing demonstrates 98.4% uniform gas distribution, resolving the technological uncertainty. Concurrently, for Component 201-B, controls engineers run Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) fault-injection simulations comparing standard PID control loops against a fuzzy-logic predictive quench algorithm, logging test results in Git version-control commits. Shop-floor machinists and technicians swipe badge IDs directly onto barcode travelers #EXP-201A-1 and #EXP-201A-2 when machining experimental vanes, assembling the test loop, and replacing fouled catalyst test coupons. Each traveler is co-signed weekly by the Lead Process Engineer, creating an unimpeachable contemporaneous record of direct support and direct engagement under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c).
Step 3: Substantiating Supply QREs and the 80% Numerator Calculation

Vanguard segregates the $85,000 of specialized ceramic guard-bed media, sacrificial catalyst cartridges poisoned during flow-loop trials, and custom helical steel vanes under an Experimental Material Requisition (EMR-201A), completely separating them from the $1,165,000 commercial vessel BOM. Step 4: Audit-Ready Substantiation Binders and Litigation Preservation Protocol

To avoid the procedural and briefing disputes that arose in the later stages of Intermountain Electronics—specifically the May 30, 2024 Rule 91(f) stipulation dispute and the August 24, 2026 Loper Bright waiver—Vanguard must institute a formal Contemporaneous Audit and Litigation Readiness Protocol. At the close of each tax year, Vanguard’s tax department must compile a self-contained digital binder for each discrete business component (201-A and 201-B). Each binder must contain a master index cross-referencing the executed contract and IP/risk addendum, the initial engineering uncertainty statement, the competing CAD/CFD design iterations, the signed #EXP shop-floor travelers and payroll registers, the EMR supply invoices, and the quantitative flow-loop test logs. This organized record structure enables tax litigation counsel to stipulate cleanly to indexed exhibits under Tax Court Rule 91(a) without needing to litigate a Rule 91(f) motion to compel stipulation.

Finally, in the event of litigation, Vanguard’s tax controversy counsel must maintain a formal issue-preservation protocol ensuring that any statutory challenge to the validity of Treasury Regulations under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo—such as challenging rigid regulatory interpretations of the "substantially all" fraction under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) or pilot model supply rules under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4)—is explicitly pleaded in the Pre-Trial Memorandum and fully briefed in the Seriatim Opening Brief, thereby preventing procedural waiver under Considine v. Commissioner.
